q: According to Coulomb's law, the electrostatic force between two point charges is:
o: Directly proportional to the sum of the charges and inversely proportional to the distance between them
Directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them
Inversely proportional to the product of the charges and directly proportional to the square of the distance
Directly proportional to the product of the charges and independent of the distance between them
x: Coulomb's law: F = kq₁q₂/r². The force depends on the product of the charges and falls off as the inverse square of their separation.

q: The electric field intensity at a point is defined as:
o: The force experienced by a unit positive test charge placed at that point
The work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point
The total charge per unit area at that point
The force experienced by an electron placed at that point
x: Electric field intensity E = F/q₀, the force per unit positive test charge. Work per unit charge from infinity defines electric potential, not field.

q: A negatively charged oil drop of mass 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held at rest in a vertical electric field of 1 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. How many excess electrons does it carry? (g = 10 m s⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
x: Balance: qE = mg, so q = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 10)/(1 × 10⁴) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁸ C. Number of electrons = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁸/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 10.

q: The electric potential at a point is defined as:
o: The force on a unit positive charge at that point
The work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point
The charge stored per unit volt at that point
The work done in moving a unit positive charge from that point to the nearest charge
x: Electric potential V = W/q₀, the work done per unit positive charge in bringing it from infinity to the point. Force per unit charge is the electric field.

q: A capacitor C is charged or discharged through a resistor R. The time constant of the circuit is:
x: The time constant is τ = RC. It is the time scale on which the capacitor charges or discharges.

q: Two point charges exert a force F on each other. If the distance between them is doubled while the charges stay the same, the force becomes:
x: F ∝ 1/r², so doubling r makes the force (½)² = ¼ of its value, F/4. F/2 is the result of forgetting to square.

q: The SI unit of electric field intensity, N C⁻¹, is equivalent to:
x: N C⁻¹ = (J m⁻¹) C⁻¹ = (J C⁻¹) m⁻¹ = V m⁻¹. J C⁻¹ is the volt itself, the unit of potential.

q: Which statement about electric potential is correct?
o: It is a vector quantity directed along the field
It has the same unit as electric field
x: Potential is work per unit charge, and work is a scalar, so potential is a scalar. It can be negative (near negative charges), and its unit is the volt, not N C⁻¹.

q: The product RC (ohm × farad) has the unit of:
x: Ω × F = (V A⁻¹)(C V⁻¹) = C A⁻¹ = (A s)/A = s. So RC is a time, measured in seconds.

q: Two point charges repel each other with force F. If each charge is doubled and the distance between them is halved, the new force is:
x: F ∝ q₁q₂/r². Doubling both charges multiplies F by 4; halving r multiplies it by another 4. New force = 16F.

q: An electron is placed in a uniform electric field that points due east. The electric force on the electron is directed:
o: Perpendicular to the field, into the page
x: The force on a charge is F = qE. For a negative charge, F is opposite to E, so the force on the electron is due west.

q: Bringing a charge of +2 μC from infinity to point P requires 6 × 10⁻⁶ J of work. The electric potential at P is:
x: V = W/q = 6 × 10⁻⁶/2 × 10⁻⁶ = 3 V. 12 V results from multiplying instead of dividing.

q: A 5 μF capacitor is charged through a 2 MΩ resistor. The time constant is:
x: τ = RC = (2 × 10⁶ Ω)(5 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 10 s. The mega and micro prefixes cancel.

q: Two point charges of 1 μC and 2 μC are placed 3 cm apart in air. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the force between them is:
x: F = kq₁q₂/r² = (9 × 10⁹)(1 × 10⁻⁶)(2 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.03)² = 1.8 × 10⁻²/9 × 10⁻⁴ = 20 N. 0.6 N comes from not squaring the distance.

q: A charge of 2 μC is placed at a point where the electric field intensity is 5 × 10³ N C⁻¹. The force on the charge is:
x: F = qE = (2 × 10⁻⁶)(5 × 10³) = 1 × 10⁻² N. 4 × 10⁻¹⁰ N comes from dividing q by E instead of multiplying.

q: Moving a charge of +5 μC from point Y to point X requires 20 μJ of work against the electric field. The potential difference V_X − V_Y is:
x: V_X − V_Y = W/q = 20 × 10⁻⁶/5 × 10⁻⁶ = +4 V. Work had to be done on the positive charge to move it to X, so X is at the higher potential.

q: When an uncharged capacitor is charged through a resistor, after a time equal to one time constant the charge on it reaches about:
x: During charging q = q₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)). At t = RC, q = q₀(1 − 0.37) ≈ 0.63q₀. 37% is the fraction left after one time constant of discharging.

q: Two charges exert a force F on each other in vacuum. They are placed, at the same separation, in a medium of relative permittivity 4. The force between them becomes:
x: In a medium F_med = F_vac/εr, so the force becomes F/4. A medium always reduces the force because εr is greater than 1.

q: The electric field due to a point charge is E at a distance r. At a distance 3r from the same charge, the field is:
x: For a point charge E = kq/r², so E ∝ 1/r². Tripling the distance gives E/3² = E/9.

q: In defining the electric potential due to a point charge, the potential is taken as zero:
o: At the position of the charge
At a distance of 1 m from the charge
x: Potential is defined as work done bringing unit positive charge from infinity, so the reference (zero) potential is at infinity, where the charge has no effect.

q: A charged capacitor discharges through a resistor. After one time constant, the charge remaining on it is about:
x: During discharge q = q₀e^(−t/RC). At t = RC, q = q₀/e ≈ 0.37q₀, about 37% of the initial charge.

q: The permittivity of free space ε₀ has the value:
x: ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻². The value 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² is the Coulomb constant k = 1/4πε₀, not ε₀ itself.

q: What is the magnitude of the electric field at a distance of 3 cm from a point charge of 1 nC? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
x: E = kq/r² = (9 × 10⁹)(1 × 10⁻⁹)/(0.03)² = 9/9 × 10⁻⁴ = 1 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. 3 × 10² N C⁻¹ results from not squaring r.

q: When released from rest in an electric field, an electron tends to move:
o: From high potential to low potential
From low potential to high potential
Only perpendicular to the field lines
x: A positive charge moves naturally from high to low potential; a negative charge such as an electron does the opposite, moving towards higher potential (against the field).

q: While a capacitor charges through a resistor from a battery, the charging current:
o: Stays constant until the capacitor is full
Is zero at first and rises to a maximum
Is maximum at the start and decreases to zero
x: At the start the capacitor has no voltage, so the current is largest (E/R). As charge builds up, the capacitor's voltage opposes the battery and the current falls towards zero.

q: A charge +2q and a charge +q are a fixed distance apart. If the force on +2q due to +q is F, the force on +q due to +2q is:
x: Coulomb forces obey Newton's third law: the two charges exert equal and opposite forces on each other, whatever their sizes. So the force is F, opposite in direction.

q: When measuring an electric field, the test charge used should be very small because:
o: A small charge experiences a larger force
The field exists only near small charges
A large charge cannot experience any force
A large charge would itself disturb the field being measured
x: A large test charge would push the source charges and alter the very field we want to measure. A tiny test charge measures the field without changing it noticeably.

q: Two parallel plates 2 cm apart have a potential difference of 200 V between them. The uniform electric field between the plates is:
x: In a uniform field E = ΔV/d = 200/0.02 = 1 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. 1 × 10² V m⁻¹ comes from using 2 instead of 0.02 m.

q: In an RC circuit the resistance is doubled while the capacitance is unchanged. The capacitor now charges:
o: Twice as fast, because the time constant is halved
Twice as slowly, because the time constant is doubled
x: τ = RC, so doubling R doubles the time constant. The capacitor takes twice as long to reach the same fraction of its final charge.

q: Two charges repel each other with a force of 3.2 N in air. When the same charges at the same separation are placed in a liquid, the force becomes 0.04 N. The relative permittivity of the liquid is:
x: εr = F_air/F_medium = 3.2/0.04 = 80. Relative permittivity of a medium is always greater than 1, so 0.0125 (the inverse ratio) is impossible.

q: A small test charge at a point in an electric field experiences force F. If the test charge is doubled, the electric field intensity at that point:
x: Doubling q₀ doubles the force F, so E = F/q₀ is unchanged. The field depends only on the source charges and the position, not on the test charge.

q: Point X is at a potential of +20 V and point Y at −10 V. How much work does the electric field do when a charge of +3 μC moves from X to Y?
x: Work done by the field = q(V_X − V_Y) = 3 × 10⁻⁶ × (20 − (−10)) = 3 × 10⁻⁶ × 30 = 9 × 10⁻⁵ J. Using 20 − 10 = 10 V gives the wrong 3 × 10⁻⁵ J.

q: A charged capacitor discharges through a resistor. Taking e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37, the charge remaining after two time constants is about:
x: q = q₀e^(−2) = q₀ × (0.37)² ≈ 0.135q₀, about 13.5%. Discharge is exponential, so the charge does not fall by equal amounts (26%) in each time constant.

q: Which statement about the relative permittivity εr of a medium is correct?
o: It has the unit C² N⁻¹ m⁻²
It equals the force between two charges in the medium divided by the force in vacuum
It is the ratio ε/ε₀ and has no unit
It is less than 1 for insulating media
x: εr = ε/ε₀ is a ratio of two permittivities, so it is dimensionless. It equals F_vacuum/F_medium (not the other way round) and is greater than 1 for every material medium.

q: Which statement correctly describes the electric field as a field of force?
o: It exists around a charge only when a second charge is placed nearby
It is the region around a charge in which another charge experiences a force
It is a scalar quantity that has magnitude only
x: An electric field is the region around a charge where any other charge experiences an electric force. It exists whether or not a test charge is present, and it is a vector.

q: Charges of +4 μC at point P and +1 μC at point R are 30 cm apart. A small charge placed on the line PR, between P and R, feels zero net electric force. Its distance from P is:
x: For zero force k(4)/x² = k(1)/(30 − x)², so x/(30 − x) = √4 = 2, giving x = 20 cm. Forgetting the square root gives x/(30 − x) = 4, x = 24 cm; the null point lies nearer the smaller charge, so 10 cm is reversed.

q: Charges of +3 μC and −4 μC are 30 cm apart in air. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the force between them is:
x: F = kq₁q₂/r² = 9 × 10⁹ × 3 × 10⁻⁶ × 4 × 10⁻⁶ / (0.3)² = 0.108/0.09 = 1.2 N, attractive because the charges are unlike. Forgetting to square r gives 0.36 N; leaving r in cm gives 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ N.

q: A charge of +2 μC is at point P and a charge of −2 μC is at point R, 20 cm apart. A charge of +1 μC is placed at the midpoint of PR. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the net force on it is:
x: Each charge is 0.1 m away: F = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ × 1 × 10⁻⁶/(0.1)² = 1.8 N. P repels it towards R and R attracts it towards R, so the forces add: 3.6 N towards R. Treating them as opposite gives zero.

q: In Coulomb's law F = kq₁q₂/r², the SI unit of the constant k is:
x: k = Fr²/(q₁q₂), so its unit is N × m²/C² = N m² C⁻². C² N⁻¹ m⁻² is the unit of ε₀, since k = 1/4πε₀.

q: Two equal point charges 1 m apart in air repel each other with a force of 9 × 10⁻³ N. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², each charge is:
x: q² = Fr²/k = 9 × 10⁻³ × 1/(9 × 10⁹) = 10⁻¹², so q = 10⁻⁶ C = 1 μC. Forgetting to take the square root gives 10⁻¹² C = 1 pC.

q: The electric field 20 cm from a point charge is 9 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the charge is:
x: q = Er²/k = 9 × 10⁵ × (0.2)²/(9 × 10⁹) = 9 × 10⁵ × 0.04/(9 × 10⁹) = 4 × 10⁻⁶ C = 4 μC. Using r instead of r² gives 20 μC.

q: Equal charges of +3 nC are placed at points P and R. Point Q is 3 cm from each, and angle PQR is 90°. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the magnitude of the resultant electric field at Q is about:
x: Each charge gives E = 9 × 10⁹ × 3 × 10⁻⁹/(0.03)² = 27/(9 × 10⁻⁴) = 3 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹, and the two fields at Q are at right angles, so the resultant is √2 × 3 × 10⁴ ≈ 4.2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. Adding them as if parallel gives 6 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹.

q: A closed surface encloses a net charge of 8.85 nC. Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², the total electric flux through the surface is:
x: Gauss's law: Φ = q/ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻⁹/(8.85 × 10⁻¹²) = 1.0 × 10³ N m² C⁻¹, whatever the shape of the surface. Inverting the ratio gives 10⁻³; using kq gives about 80.

q: A point charge q is placed at the centre of a cube. The electric flux through any one face of the cube is:
x: By Gauss's law the total flux through the closed cube is q/ε₀. By symmetry the six faces share it equally, so each face has q/6ε₀.

q: A flat surface of area 0.5 m² is placed in a uniform electric field of 200 N C⁻¹. The normal to the surface makes an angle of 60° with the field. The electric flux through the surface is:
x: Φ = EA cos θ = 200 × 0.5 × cos 60° = 100 × 0.5 = 50 N m² C⁻¹, where θ is between the field and the normal (vector area). Using sin 60° gives about 87; ignoring the angle gives 100.

q: A positive charge is given to a hollow closed metal box. The electric field at points in the empty space inside the box is:
o: Equal to the field just outside the surface
x: The charge on a conductor sits on its outer surface, and a Gaussian surface inside the cavity encloses no charge, so the field inside is zero. This is why a Faraday cage shields what is inside.

q: An electron is placed in a uniform electric field of 910 N C⁻¹. Taking e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and ignoring gravity, the magnitude of its acceleration is:
x: a = F/m = eE/m = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 910/(9.1 × 10⁻³¹) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10³³ = 1.6 × 10¹⁴ m s⁻². Multiplying by the mass instead of dividing gives the absurd 1.3 × 10⁻⁴⁶.

q: Two large parallel metal plates carry equal and opposite surface charge densities of magnitude 8.85 × 10⁻⁸ C m⁻². Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², the electric field between the plates is:
x: Between oppositely charged plates E = σ/ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻⁸/(8.85 × 10⁻¹²) = 1.0 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ (the two sheets' fields of σ/2ε₀ each add). Using σ/2ε₀ for one sheet gives 5.0 × 10³ N C⁻¹.

q: Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the electric potential 30 cm from a point charge of +2 nC is:
x: V = kq/r = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁹/0.3 = 18/0.3 = 60 V. Dividing by r² gives 200 V; leaving r in cm gives 0.6 V.

q: Charges of +5 nC and −5 nC are fixed 10 cm apart. At the midpoint between them:
o: Both the potential and the electric field are zero
The electric field is zero but the potential is not zero
Neither the potential nor the electric field is zero
The potential is zero but the electric field is not zero
x: Potential is a scalar: kq/r + k(−q)/r = 0. The fields are vectors that both point from the positive towards the negative charge, so they add and the field is not zero.

q: An electron starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 500 V. Taking e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the kinetic energy it gains is:
x: KE = eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 500 = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ J (that is, 500 eV). Dividing e by V gives 3.2 × 10⁻²²; dividing V by e gives 3.1 × 10²¹.

q: A proton starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 5000 V. Taking its mass as 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, its final speed is:
x: ½mv² = eV, so v² = 2eV/m = 2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5000/(1.6 × 10⁻²⁷) = 10¹² and v = 1.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. Dropping the 2 gives about 7.1 × 10⁵; forgetting the square root gives 10¹².

q: In a uniform electric field, neighbouring equipotential surfaces 2 V apart are 1 cm apart. The electric field is:
o: 200 V m⁻¹, pointing towards lower potential
200 V m⁻¹, pointing towards higher potential
2 V m⁻¹, pointing towards lower potential
0.02 V m⁻¹, pointing towards lower potential
x: E = −ΔV/Δr: magnitude 2 V/0.01 m = 200 V m⁻¹, and the minus sign means it points in the direction in which the potential falls. Leaving the distance in cm gives 2 V m⁻¹.

q: Two point charges of +2 μC and +3 μC are 30 cm apart. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², their electric potential energy is:
x: U = kq₁q₂/r = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ × 3 × 10⁻⁶/0.3 = 0.054/0.3 = 0.18 J, positive because like charges repel. Dividing by r² gives 0.60 J; forgetting to divide by r gives 0.054 J.

q: Point X is 30 cm from a +6 nC charge and 10 cm from a −2 nC charge. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the work needed to bring a +1 μC charge slowly from infinity to X is:
x: V_X = 9 × 10⁹ × 6 × 10⁻⁹/0.3 + 9 × 10⁹ × (−2 × 10⁻⁹)/0.1 = 180 − 180 = 0 V, so W = qV = 0. Potentials add as scalars, so directions do not matter; adding the magnitudes gives 360 V and 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ J.

q: One electron volt (1 eV) is equal to:
x: 1 eV is the energy gained by one electronic charge moving through 1 V: W = qV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C × 1 V = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ J is 1 keV.

q: At a distance r from a point charge, the electric potential is V and the field strength is E. At a distance 2r from the same charge, the potential and field strength are:
x: V = kq/r falls as 1/r, so it halves; E = kq/r² falls as 1/r², so it becomes a quarter. Mixing up the two dependences gives V/4 and E/2.

q: In a Millikan experiment an oil drop of mass 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held at rest between horizontal plates 1 cm apart with 2000 V across them. Taking g = 10 m s⁻² and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the number of excess electrons on the drop is:
x: E = V/d = 2000/0.01 = 2 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹; qE = mg gives q = 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁴/(2 × 10⁵) = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C = 3e. Leaving d in cm gives E = 2000 and 300 electrons.

q: In Millikan's experiment, with the electric field switched off, an oil drop soon falls at a constant (terminal) speed because:
o: The electric force on it becomes zero
Gravity does not act on such a small drop
Its weight is balanced by the viscous drag of the air
x: As the drop speeds up, the viscous drag F = 6πηrv grows until it equals the weight mg (upthrust ignored); the net force is then zero and the speed stays constant. With the field off there is no electric force at all.

q: In Millikan's experiment an oil drop of density 900 kg m⁻³ falls with a terminal speed of 1.0 × 10⁻³ m s⁻¹ through air of viscosity 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ N s m⁻². Using mg = 6πηrv, with g = 10 m s⁻² and upthrust ignored, the radius of the drop is:
x: (4/3)πr³ρg = 6πηrv gives r² = 9ηv/(2ρg) = 9 × 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 10⁻³/(2 × 900 × 10) = 9 × 10⁻¹², so r = 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ m. Forgetting the square root gives 9 × 10⁻¹²; dropping the 2 gives about 4.2 × 10⁻⁶ m.

q: Millikan found that the charge on any oil drop is a whole-number multiple of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Which of these could be the charge on a drop?
x: 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁹/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4, a whole number. The others give 1.5, 3.5 and about 0.6 electron charges, which are impossible because charge is quantised.

q: A parallel-plate capacitor in air has plates of area 1 m² separated by 1 mm. Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, its capacitance is:
x: C = ε₀A/d = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 1/(1 × 10⁻³) = 8.85 × 10⁻⁹ F = 8.85 nF. Ignoring the mm-to-m conversion gives 8.85 pF; inverting the formula gives about 1.1 × 10⁸ F.

q: A 10 μF air capacitor stays connected to a 12 V battery while a slab of dielectric constant 3 is pushed in to fill the space between its plates. The charge on the capacitor becomes:
x: With the battery connected V stays 12 V, while C becomes 3 × 10 = 30 μF, so Q = CV = 30 × 12 = 360 μC. 120 μC is the charge before the dielectric; 40 μC wrongly divides by 3.

q: A 4 μF capacitor is charged to 100 V and then disconnected from the battery. A dielectric of dielectric constant 2 is then made to fill the space between its plates. The energy stored becomes:
x: Initially U = ½CV² = ½ × 4 × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁴ = 0.02 J. Isolated, Q stays fixed and C doubles, so U = Q²/2C halves to 0.01 J. Assuming V stays fixed (battery connected) gives 0.04 J.

q: Capacitors of 3 μF and 6 μF are connected in series across a 12 V battery. The potential difference across the 3 μF capacitor is:
x: Series: C = 3 × 6/(3 + 6) = 2 μF, Q = 2 × 12 = 24 μC on each; V across 3 μF = 24/3 = 8 V (and 4 V across 6 μF, total 12 V). Swapping the two gives 4 V; the smaller capacitor takes the larger p.d.

q: Two 4 μF capacitors are connected in parallel, and this pair is connected in series with an 8 μF capacitor. The equivalent capacitance of the combination is:
x: The parallel pair gives 4 + 4 = 8 μF; 8 μF in series with 8 μF gives 8 × 8/(8 + 8) = 4 μF. Putting all three in parallel gives 16 μF; all in series gives 1.6 μF.

q: A 20 μF capacitor is charged to a potential difference of 200 V. The energy stored in it is:
x: U = ½CV² = ½ × 20 × 10⁻⁶ × (200)² = 10 × 10⁻⁶ × 4 × 10⁴ = 0.4 J. Forgetting the ½ gives 0.8 J; forgetting to square V gives 0.002 J; ignoring the μ gives 4 × 10⁵ J.

q: Which change doubles the capacitance of a parallel-plate air capacitor?
o: Doubling the area of each plate
Doubling the separation of the plates
Doubling the charge on the plates
Doubling the potential difference across the plates
x: C = ε₀A/d depends only on the geometry (and the medium): doubling A doubles C, doubling d halves it. Changing Q or V changes the other in the same ratio and leaves C unchanged.

q: A 10 μF capacitor charged to 50 V is discharged through a 100 kΩ resistor. Taking e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37, the potential difference across the capacitor after 1 s is about:
x: τ = RC = 100 × 10³ × 10 × 10⁻⁶ = 1 s, so after 1 s V = 50 × e⁻¹ ≈ 50 × 0.37 = 18.5 V. 31.5 V is the 63% figure that belongs to charging; 6.8 V is the value after two time constants.

q: The farad, the SI unit of capacitance, is equal to:
x: C = Q/V, so 1 F = 1 coulomb per volt = 1 C V⁻¹. J C⁻¹ is the volt itself.
